learnings.learning: Explicit drug cross-category boosting hurts performance (-0.74pp) - kNN already captures this signal
learnings.implication: Category-based boosting should be at disease/prediction level, not drug level

learnings.learning: Incoherent predictions at GOLDEN/HIGH tiers should be demoted. This improved GOLDEN precision by +7.78 pp (22.48% → 30.26%).
learnings.implication: ATC coherence is both a positive signal (h309/h310 boost) AND negative signal (h311 demotion). The optimal strategy uses coherence bidirectionally.

learnings.learning: ATC mismatches are not uniformly bad. D→respiratory (27.5%) and A→ophthalmological (26.5%) outperform coherent baseline (11.7%). Meanwhile A→cancer, J→cancer, N→cancer have 0% precision.
learnings.implication: Refine h311 demotion to only demote truly harmful mismatches (A/J/N→cancer, etc.) and rescue surprisingly good mismatches (D→respiratory, etc.).

learnings.learning: Zero-precision ATC mismatches (A/J/N→cancer, etc.) should always be FILTERED. 1,319 predictions had only 1.21% precision. High-precision mismatches (10-27%) should NOT be rescued since they are still below GOLDEN baseline (30%).
learnings.implication: ATC coherence is now a 3-level signal: coherent (GOLDEN), incoherent-but-not-zero (demote to HIGH), zero-precision (FILTER).

learnings.learning: J (antibiotic) drugs have 0% precision for 9 disease categories. Only J→respiratory (17.8%) and J→other (7.4%) are acceptable. Comprehensive ATC class filters are highly effective.
learnings.implication: Expand comprehensive filtering to N, L, C drug classes. Each ATC class has predictable cross-domain failure patterns.

learnings.learning: 43 total ATC→category pairs now filter ~2,200 predictions with <1% precision. Major drug class cross-domain failures are: L (antineoplastics) for non-cancer, N (neurological) for non-neuro, C (cardiovascular) for non-CV.
learnings.implication: ATC L1 coherence is highly predictive of precision. Production system should prioritize same-domain predictions.

learnings.learning: kNN success is bimodal (100% or 0%) and category-driven. Existing tier system is well-aligned. Pool size adds minimal predictive value.
learnings.implication: Focus on improving category-specific rules rather than per-disease calibration. Consider promoting cancer/endocrine to higher tiers.

learnings.learning: Class width does NOT predict isolation signal. Most classes benefit from cohesion. Platinum agents are unique exception (isolation=good) due to cancer-selectivity.
learnings.implication: Current broad class isolation demotion is correct. Consider platinum isolation boost. Statin exception was spurious (small n).

learnings.learning: Category-specific coherence varies from +25pp (ophthalmic) to -7pp (renal). Cancer has no coherence signal. Renal is inverted.
learnings.implication: Uniform demotion suboptimal. Category-specific rules could improve cancer/metabolic/renal predictions.

learnings.learning: ACE inhibitors show opposite cohesion pattern to statins (-22.2pp gap vs +16.7pp). Anti-VEGF cancer drugs (Bevacizumab) can be repurposed for inflammatory diseases (psoriatic arthritis) where VEGF is elevated. Case report evidence: PMC4248526.
learnings.implication: Drug class cohesion patterns are heterogeneous - statins are exception not rule. Anti-VEGF mechanism is promising for inflammatory disease repurposing.

learnings.learning: Anti-VEGF drugs (bevacizumab, sunitinib, sorafenib) have case report evidence for psoriasis efficacy. MEK inhibitors are cancer-specific (0% non-cancer precision). Drug mechanism class determines repurposing potential.
learnings.implication: VEGF inhibition is a valid mechanism for psoriasis repurposing. MEK inhibition is not. Mechanism-based drug classification improves prediction quality.

learnings.learning: Cancer drug cross-activity patterns: ALL mechanisms show 0-2.6% non-cancer precision. kNN predicts by disease similarity, not drug mechanism. High-indication drugs (steroids, antibiotics) are noise in LOW tier, signal in HIGH tier.
learnings.implication: Consider cancer drug filter; avoid indication-count boosting; kNN fundamentally limited for mechanism-based repurposing

learnings.learning: Organ proximity does NOT predict drug transferability. Within-organ novel predictions have 1.2% precision. Only pathway-comprehensive mechanisms (like statins for CV) transfer reliably.
learnings.implication: Do not use organ matching as confidence signal. Focus on identifying pathway-comprehensive drug classes.

learnings.learning: Pathway-comprehensive drugs (treat base AND complications) have 48.8% precision for CV complications vs 7.6% for non-pathway-comprehensive (6.4x lift). But this pattern does NOT hold for renal complications (-6 pp).
learnings.implication: CV complication predictions should check for pathway-comprehensive status. Renal complications need different approach.

learnings.learning: Model correctly predicted 5/9 emerging treatments (55%). Validated: Sotatercept→PAH (FDA 2024), Dantrolene→VT (RCT 2025), Canagliflozin→HF (HIGH). Missed: newer drugs not in DRKG, some SGLT2→HF patterns.
learnings.implication: Model has good signal for drugs in DRKG. Coverage gap for newer drugs. SGLT2→HF gap suggests kNN disease similarity issue.

learnings.learning: SGLT2→HF 'gap' was a misunderstanding. Empagliflozin HF is in GT, so correctly filtered from novel predictions. Canagliflozin→chronic HF IS predicted at HIGH. Deliverables may need regeneration to reflect latest GOLDEN rules.
learnings.implication: Check assumptions before investigating gaps. Known indications are correctly filtered from deliverables.

learnings.learning: DRKG coverage gap is 66.5% of GT drugs (1,574/2,367) missing. Gap is structural - DRKG vintage (~2020) misses newer drugs. Best coverage for established classes (statins 82%, ACE-i 78%), worst for newer classes (DPP4i 5.3%, SGLT2i 26.3%).
learnings.implication: Model limitations are primarily coverage, not algorithm. Consider manual rules for high-impact missing drug classes or DRKG update.

learnings.learning: Tier system is well-calibrated: HIGH(15% known) > MEDIUM(7.2%) > LOW(1.5%). However, LOW tier may contain valid drugs with sparse DRKG connectivity (e.g., Landiolol - FDA-approved but LOW tier due to only 6 predictions).
learnings.implication: Consider sparse drug rescue mechanism. Don't dismiss LOW tier entirely.

learnings.learning: DPP4 '5.3% coverage' was a measurement artifact from stale deliverables. DPP4 drugs ARE properly in DRKG (600-1700 edges), GT, and embeddings. After regeneration, Sitagliptin/Saxagliptin appear at GOLDEN tier for diabetes.
learnings.implication: Never trust coverage measurements against old deliverables. Always regenerate before measuring.

learnings.learning: Target-based scoring and kNN achieve equivalent performance on cancer diseases (65.8% vs 63.2%), but win on different diseases (18 shared, 7 target-only, 6 kNN-only). This suggests complementary signals worth ensembling.
learnings.implication: Focus on ensembling rather than replacing kNN with target-based approach.

learnings.learning: Max ensemble of target overlap and kNN achieves 76.3% R@30 on cancer diseases (+10.5 pp over best single method). Taking the max of normalized scores outperforms weighted averages or rank fusion.
learnings.implication: For cancer predictions, use max(target_score, kNN_score) to capture complementary signals from both methods.

learnings.learning: Cancer subtypes have very different optimal methods: Hematological cancers achieve 93.3% with ensemble, but Brain/CNS tumors only 25% with Target (kNN gets 50%). Sarcomas: Target-only is best (100%).
learnings.implication: Consider subtype-specific method selection for cancer predictions.

learnings.learning: MinRank ensemble (min rank from target/kNN) improves cancer (+10.5 pp) and neuro (+5.3 pp) but hurts autoimmune (-5.6 pp). Ensemble only helps when methods have equal performance.
learnings.implication: Use adaptive selection: ensemble when |target-kNN| < 10 pp, else dominant method

learnings.learning: MinRank ensemble captures complementary signals: Target uses gene overlap, kNN uses embedding similarity. Works when methods are equal (cancer, neuro). When one dominates (autoimmune: Target 89%), use dominant method alone.
learnings.implication: Production predictor should use category-specific method selection: ensemble for cancer/neuro, Target alone for autoimmune/CV

learnings.learning: Ensemble methods validated in isolation may not help in production when existing rules capture similar signals
learnings.implication: Always test improvements in full production context, not just isolated experiments

learnings.learning: GI category fails because kNN neighbors are from different categories with different drug needs
learnings.implication: Category-specific drug class injection (like h171 for neurological) can rescue low-coverage categories

learnings.learning: MinRank ensemble only helps categories where Target and kNN have similar performance. When kNN dominates, ensemble hurts by mixing noise from weaker Target method.
learnings.implication: Apply ensemble selectively to autoimmune/metabolic/cancer only. This reinforces h369/h370/h374.

learnings.learning: HIGH tier actually has higher precision than GOLDEN (59.9% vs 35.8%). Several category hierarchy rules (CV, thyroid) are too broad.
learnings.implication: Need to tighten GOLDEN criteria or demote some GOLDEN rules to HIGH.

learnings.learning: Viral diseases (hepatitis, HIV) have 0% infectious rule precision. Bacterial-specific rules (UTI, TB) work well (45-75%). General infectious GOLDEN rule should be removed.
learnings.implication: Split infectious category into viral vs bacterial for tier rules.

learnings.learning: Removing low-precision rules (infectious GOLDEN at 5.3%, viral hierarchies at 0%) improved GOLDEN tier precision by +4.6pp.
learnings.implication: Continue auditing and removing problem rules identified in h378.

learnings.learning: Category-specific ensemble routing improves raw LOO (+1.5pp) but HURTS production (-2.9pp) because rank changes disrupt tier rules. Production tier rules already capture target overlap signal.
learnings.implication: Never evaluate rank-changing interventions with raw LOO alone - must test in full production context with tier rules. Use target overlap as tier signal, not rank modifier.

learnings.learning: Target overlap should be used as tier promotion signal (adjusting confidence) not rank modifier (changing drug order). Same signal, opposite effects on production quality.
learnings.implication: Always test confidence interventions in production context, not just raw LOO. Rank changes disrupt tier rules but tier promotions compose cleanly.

learnings.learning: 7 below-tier rules were dragging precision down. Largest impact: cancer cross-type at MEDIUM (0.9%, n=349), hematological at HIGH (19.1%, n=94). Demoting to appropriate tiers improved HIGH by +7.9pp.
learnings.implication: Regularly audit per-rule precision within each tier. Rules that were accurate when first created may drift as other rules change the prediction pool.

learnings.learning: Frequency leakage inflates R@30 by 4.0pp and HIGH precision by 2.7pp. GOLDEN is almost unaffected (-0.4pp). In production (new diseases), there is no leakage.
learnings.implication: Report honest R@30 as ~75% not 79%. Tier precision numbers are ~1-3pp optimistic but directionally correct.

learnings.learning: Holdout validation shows tier system is genuine (HIGH/MED/LOW retain >80% precision) but GOLDEN tier is misnomered. GOLDEN<HIGH inversion is real, not overfitting artifact. Most "overfitted" hierarchy rules are structural absence (1-disease groups cannot be holdout-tested). cancer_same_type has moderate GT leakage (-5.8pp).
learnings.implication: Fix GOLDEN by raising its threshold or merging with HIGH. h396 is critical. For hierarchy rules with 1 disease, consider literature validation instead of holdout.

learnings.learning: GOLDEN<HIGH inversion was caused by cancer_same_type (24.5% precision) comprising 57% of GOLDEN. Demoting to MEDIUM fixed ordering and raised GOLDEN to 53.6%. High-precision rules should dominate GOLDEN, not high-volume mediocre rules.
learnings.implication: When adding new GOLDEN rules, verify their precision exceeds current HIGH tier average (~48%). Volume dilutes precision.

learnings.learning: Category-specific k values (h66) are invalidated in production because h170 selective boosting already provides category focus. Reducing k from 20 to 5/10 removes useful diverse neighbors. Only cancer benefits from k=30.
learnings.implication: Do not deploy category-specific k. h170 boosting is sufficient for category routing. Future k optimization should account for all production features.

learnings.learning: Target overlap promotions are genuine. HIGH→GOLDEN (78.5%, n=93) is very strong. LOW→MEDIUM drops -12.6pp on holdout but remains 13.3pp above tier average. Some circularity expected since drug-disease treatment edges create target overlap.
learnings.implication: Do not remove overlap promotions. For future rules using drug-disease similarity signals, expect ~10-15pp holdout degradation from partial circularity.

learnings.learning: Rule ordering in _assign_confidence_tier has a critical gap: the rank>20 filter fires BEFORE high-precision hierarchy/pathway rules, throwing away 332 predictions at 60.5% precision. Moving these checks before the rank filter recovers 201 GT hits with GOLDEN +2.1pp and HIGH +0.2pp improvement.
learnings.implication: When adding new rules, always check if they should fire before or after the rank>20 filter. High-precision domain-specific rules should generally override rank filtering.

learnings.learning: ATC L1 mismatch rules are too coarse. Many valid drug-disease pairs share ATC categories that seem wrong at L1 level but make sense clinically (e.g., corticosteroids=ATC A for nephrotic syndrome, opioids=ATC R for pain). Consider L2/L3 refinement for remaining borderline rules.
learnings.implication: When designing cross-category filters, use the most specific classification level available. L1 ATC codes lose too much nuance.

learnings.learning: FILTER and LOW precision converge at ~12% because rank>20 predictions (13.1% precision) dominate FILTER. The genuine FILTER patterns (cross_domain 0%, cancer_no_gt 1.6%) are diluted by the high-volume standard FILTER. The tier distinction is still meaningful for the specific zero-precision patterns.
learnings.implication: Report FILTER precision excluding the standard rank>20 pool to give users a more accurate picture of what FILTER means.

learnings.learning: Rule coverage analysis revealed: 71% of predictions go through standard path (no specific rule fires). Psychiatric category is dramatically under-served by rules (53% MEDIUM precision via overlap promotion should be HIGH/GOLDEN). Incoherent_demotion needs category-specific handling. Infectious low-rank (1-5) has 43% precision despite being in LOW tier.
learnings.implication: Focus new rules on under-served high-precision categories: psychiatric, infectious low-rank. Category-specific rule refinements have more potential than new global rules.

learnings.learning: Rule audit found only 1 of 83 rules is clearly bad (pneumonia hierarchy). 21 rules are too small to evaluate. Code complexity comes from many small rules, not bad rules. Demoting 3 marginal rules improved HIGH by +2.5pp while maintaining tier ordering.
learnings.implication: Focus on rule CONSOLIDATION rather than pruning. Many small rules work individually but create code complexity. Minimum sample size ~30 for reliable holdout validation.

learnings.learning: Attempted T2D GOLDEN rescue failed because only 2 diseases match T2D criteria. With 80/20 holdout, too few in holdout to validate. Confirmed h402 finding: min n≈30 for reliable holdout.
learnings.implication: Do not attempt tier promotions based on 1-2 disease signals. Need at least 5+ diseases in the group for holdout reliability.

learnings.learning: Sample size determines holdout reliability: n<30 = 16-21pp degradation (unreliable), n=31-100 = 9.8pp (moderate), n>100 = 6.2pp (reliable), n>500 = 3.1pp (stable). Set minimum n=30 for any tier rule.
learnings.implication: Before adding or modifying tier rules, check n first. Rules with n<30 should not be assigned tiers based on full-data precision alone. The target_overlap_promotion rule (n=273) is an outlier with -22.5pp due to feature inflation, not sample size.

learnings.learning: LOO frequency provides negligible holdout improvement (0-0.4pp). Feature inflation via frequency is a 0.5-1pp effect; kNN neighborhood changes are the 5-10pp driver. The rank>20 filter compensates for kNN instability, not frequency inflation.
learnings.implication: To improve rank>20 predictions, need to stabilize kNN neighborhoods (bootstrap, more data, or stable ranking methods) rather than deflate features.

learnings.learning: TransE consilience (kNN ∩ TransE top-30) is a strong, holdout-validated signal: +13.6pp lift for MEDIUM tier (34.7% vs 21.2%). TransE alone is weak (5.2%) but serves as an independent validation filter. The consilience principle works: predictions agreed upon by multiple independent methods are more reliable.
learnings.implication: Implement TransE top-30 agreement as a tier promotion signal. MEDIUM + TransE top-30 → HIGH candidate. This is the first new feature to improve tier precision since h388 target overlap.

learnings.learning: Bootstrap/bagging of kNN neighborhoods HURTS performance (-1.54pp R@30, +30.5% more rank drift). Subsampling 80% of train diseases loses genuinely informative neighbors. kNN instability is structural (455 diseases, k=20) and cannot be fixed by aggregation. The rank>20 filter remains the correct response.
learnings.implication: Future rank stability work should focus on drug-level signals (embedding stability, score margins) rather than disease neighborhood manipulation. Within-tier ranking (using TransE, score margins, etc.) is more productive than trying to rescue rank 21-30.

learnings.learning: kNN rank is already the best within-tier ranking signal. TransE composite does NOT improve over kNN rank. TransE value is binary (tier indicator), not continuous (ranking signal). Top-half vs bottom-half gap on holdout: HIGH +15.9pp, MEDIUM +11.5pp. TransE boolean is actually NEGATIVE for global ranking (MEDIUM -3.7pp, LOW -4.4pp) — the h405 benefit is purely per-disease, not global.
learnings.implication: For clinical deliverables, emphasize that rank within tier is informative. Consider reporting sub-tier precision (rank 1-5 vs 6-10 vs 11-20). Do not attempt to replace kNN rank as the primary ordering signal.

learnings.learning: kNN bootstrap (subsampling 80% of training diseases per run) HURTS performance (-1.17pp holdout, -2.91pp full-data). Subsampling removes actual nearest neighbors, degrading neighborhood quality. Unlike classical bagging, kNN subsampling adds noise. Rank drift INCREASES +30.3%. The 4.1 rank-20 crossings per disease are inherent to embedding topology, not fixable by subsampling.
learnings.implication: kNN neighborhood instability is a fundamental property of the embedding space, not a sampling artifact. Do NOT attempt further subsampling-based approaches. Alternative: use neighborhood quality metrics (mean cosine similarity) as META-CONFIDENCE, or test k-expansion (consensus across multiple k values).

learnings.learning: k-expansion (multi-k Borda, multi-k averaging, k=30) does not improve R@30 (max +0.31pp) or rank stability (crossings identical). Combined with h436 (bootstrap -1.17pp), this proves kNN rank instability is an inherent embedding space property. Neither adding nor removing information changes it.
learnings.implication: The rank>20 filter is the CORRECT response to this instability. Further ranking stabilization requires fundamentally different approaches (different embedding method, different similarity metric) rather than kNN parameter tuning.

learnings.learning: Drug rank stability (CV across diseases) is entirely circular with GT: stable-rank drugs are stable BECAUSE they appear in every neighbor's GT, which is the evaluation GT. Full-data: 97.2% for Q1 vs 17.6% for Q4. Holdout: REVERSES to 7.4% vs 9.4%. Any kNN-derived drug metric is confounded by GT overlap.
learnings.implication: Do NOT use drug-level kNN metrics (rank CV, appearance frequency, rank spread) for within-tier ranking. These are all circular. Valid within-tier signals must come from EXTERNAL sources: TransE, target overlap, mechanism support, literature.

learnings.learning: Target overlap provides ~2x precision lift at all ranks (non-circular signal) but rank 31-50 base precision is too low (3-4%) for rescue. Even overlap>=5 only reaches 9.4% at rank 41-50. Top-30 hard limit is correct. Combined with h399/h418/h423/h434/h436/h451: rank>20 filter is definitively validated from 7 angles.
learnings.implication: The rank>20 filter is now EXHAUSTIVELY validated (7 independent approaches all confirm). Close this research direction permanently. Focus future work on WITHIN rank 1-20 precision improvement or external data integration.

learnings.learning: Self-referential leakage: diseases are their own #1 nearest neighbor (sim=1.0) and predict their own GT drugs. DKA has 6/7 hits purely from self-prediction, no other neighbors contribute. This inflates full-data precision but disappears on holdout. Any full-data evaluation of base_to_complication (or similar rules) that includes self-prediction is systematically inflated.
learnings.implication: Full-data precision for kNN-based rules should always be accompanied by holdout validation. Self-referential inflation is largest for diseases with unique drug signatures (no neighbor overlap). Consider excluding self-similarity in full-data evaluation or always using LOO.

learnings.learning: Circularity audit complete: 7 hierarchy rules show 0% holdout because drug_disease_groups is recomputed from training GT (structural absence, not overfitting). 19 large-n rules are genuine (gap<=10pp). The tier system has no HIDDEN circularity beyond the known small-group limitation. Target overlap promotion has -14.2pp gap (expected since overlap counts change with GT). The holdout validation framework correctly identifies both genuine and structurally limited rules.
learnings.implication: No code changes needed. The circularity is well-characterized and the correct response is MIN_N filtering (n>=30 for holdout conclusions, per h402). Small hierarchy rules cannot be holdout-validated but ARE medically correct (h432 confirmed). Future rule additions should target n>=30 predictions for reliable validation.

learnings.learning: External signals (target overlap, mechanism, frequency) do NOT add value beyond kNN rank for within-tier ordering. The tier system creates a COLLIDER EFFECT: within a tier, rank and external signals are anti-correlated because tier assignment conditions on both. Adding external signals to rank introduces noise. kNN rank IS the optimal within-tier signal.
learnings.implication: Do not attempt further within-tier reranking. The current system is already optimal. Future improvements must come from tier ASSIGNMENT (what goes into each tier) rather than within-tier ORDERING.

learnings.learning: Mean train_frequency of top-20 predictions does NOT predict disease-level R@30 after controlling for category. The apparent Q1 vs Q4 gap (+16.0pp) was entirely driven by category composition (easy=autoimmune/dermatological, hard=metabolic/neurological). Within same category, the signal reverses (-5.1pp).
learnings.implication: Always test confounders before concluding a signal is genuine. Category is the primary driver of disease difficulty.

learnings.learning: MEDIUM and FILTER tiers have reliable, monotonic rank-based precision calibration. HIGH has massive full-to-holdout gaps (up to 38.5pp at R11-15) due to hierarchy rescue effects. LOW rank calibration REVERSES on holdout (collider effect from h453). Updated RANK_BUCKET_PRECISION with 5-seed holdout values.
learnings.implication: Only present rank-bucket precision for MEDIUM tier in clinical recommendations. HIGH/LOW rank-bucket values should be treated as approximate.

learnings.learning: HIGH tier rank distortion is caused by hierarchy rescue rules that promote drugs at ALL rank positions. Hierarchy-matched drugs have ~31% precision regardless of rank (hierarchy IS the signal). Non-hierarchy HIGH predictions have clean rank gradient (31% → 11%). Rank calibration only meaningful for non-hierarchy HIGH predictions.
learnings.implication: For HIGH tier, present overall precision (31%) not rank-based calibration. Hierarchy match is binary, not graded by rank.

learnings.learning: Mean neighbor similarity is NOT a useful meta-confidence signal. Low-similarity diseases actually have HIGHER precision in GOLDEN/HIGH/FILTER because they are specific diseases rescued by hierarchy rules. The tier system COMPENSATES for kNN unreliability in sparse neighborhoods. Direction of the signal varies by tier.
learnings.implication: Do not use neighborhood density/similarity as meta-confidence. The tier system already accounts for neighborhood quality through its hierarchy and rescue rules.

learnings.learning: Category-specific MEDIUM precision varies enormously (0-47% holdout). Immunological has 36pp overfitting gap from only 5 diseases. Neurological, immunological, reproductive demoted to LOW. No category reaches HIGH threshold.
learnings.implication: Small-n categories are vulnerable to massive overfitting. Use holdout validation for any category-specific rules, especially when n_diseases < 10.

learnings.learning: 10 psychiatric diseases is insufficient for category-specific promotion (2 per holdout seed, extreme variance). Need >=50 diseases for n>=10 per seed and statistical power. Mechanism support is universal for psychiatric MEDIUM (no filtering power).
learnings.implication: Category-specific tier promotions require >=50 diseases. For small categories, use category_holdout_precision annotation instead of tier changes.

learnings.learning: Hierarchy rules encode genuine medical knowledge (14/20 confirmed by guidelines, 0 memorization). But substring matching is fragile: 3 bugs found where short variants (sle, cystitis, fibrosis) matched wrong diseases. HIERARCHY_EXCLUSIONS dict added to prevent false matches. Impact: MEDIUM +1.1pp holdout.
learnings.implication: Always audit substring matches for false positives, especially with short variant strings. Consider word-boundary matching (h469).

learnings.learning: 5 additional substring bugs found: 'tia'→'interstitial' (16 false drugs), 'pneumonia'→autoimmune pneumonia, 'diabetic'→'nondiabetic', 'diabetic'→foot infections, 'thyroid'→cancer. All short variants <=3 chars are now removed or excluded. Also found 7 category mismatches that are medically expected (not bugs).
learnings.implication: Hierarchy exclusion list is now comprehensive. No more short-variant bugs expected. Consider h469 (word-boundary matching) only if new variants are added in the future.

learnings.learning: Low-similarity diseases are COMMON diseases with unique drug profiles (hypertension, RA, diabetes), not rare diseases. Dense neighborhoods are niche infectious diseases sharing antibiotics. Correlation sim vs n_drugs = -0.395. Hierarchy coverage is 40% for sparse Q1 vs 5% for dense Q4.
learnings.implication: Sparse/dense neighborhood distinction provides no actionable signal. Hierarchy rescue for sparse diseases is expected and correct.

learnings.learning: 75% of top 20 GOLDEN novel predictions have clinical literature support (55% GT gaps, 20% promising). Extrapolating to all 104 GOLDEN novels by drug class: 92.3% have support. Major GT gap sources: corticosteroids (38%), lipid drugs (27%). Only 8% truly uncertain.
learnings.implication: GOLDEN tier is genuinely high-precision. GT incompleteness (especially for drug class members) is the primary source of 'novel' predictions. Consider class-level GT expansion.

learnings.learning: HIGH novel validation: 65% clinical support (35% GT gap, 30% promising, 25% weak, 10% HARMFUL). Found 10 inverse-indication predictions: anti-thyroid drugs→hypothyroidism, thyroid hormones→hyperthyroidism, diazoxide→hyperglycemia. Hierarchy rules don't account for opposite conditions in same organ system. Implemented INVERSE_INDICATION_PAIRS filter.
learnings.implication: Literature validation catches safety issues that holdout cannot. Hierarchy rules need systematic audit for inverse patterns. Every tier should be literature-validated.

learnings.learning: Only metabolic hierarchy groups (thyroid, diabetes) have inverse-indication issues. Root cause: hierarchy matches by organ system keyword, not drug mechanism. 26 total harmful predictions removed. Autoimmune/CV/infectious/neurological/respiratory hierarchies are clean.
learnings.implication: Inverse-indication check should be standard for any NEW hierarchy group added. Only metabolic groups need opposite-condition checking.

learnings.learning: MEDIUM tier has 52% clinical support (GT_GAP 40% + PROMISING 12%), 8% HARMFUL, 16% NO_EVIDENCE. Standard rule has 100% GT_GAP rate (7/7). Target overlap promotion and ATC coherent rules have highest false positive rates. Metronidazole→myopia and verapamil→cardiac arrest are new inverse indications.
learnings.implication: Standard rule predictions are the most reliable in MEDIUM tier. Target overlap promotion needs audit. Literature validation should continue for cancer_same_type and ATC coherent rules. SIDER database could systematically identify inverse indications.

learnings.learning: Corticosteroid iatrogenic filter was incomplete: cortisone/mometasone/fludrocortisone missing from CORTICOSTEROID_DRUGS. Pancreatitis is a dual case (steroids cause drug-induced pancreatitis but treat autoimmune pancreatitis). Generic pancreatitis → FILTER is correct since autoimmune pancreatitis is a specific subtype.
learnings.implication: When adding drugs to reference sets, verify completeness. Drug classes often have members that were missed in initial curation. Dual-use drugs (cause and treat related conditions) need careful handling.

learnings.learning: Target overlap promotion is actually the 3rd best MEDIUM rule (35.9% holdout), contradicting h483's small sample. However, cancer cross-type overlap promotion has 0.3% holdout - blocking cancer from promotion yields MEDIUM +1.4pp. Lesson: always validate rules with holdout, not small literature samples.
learnings.implication: Rule evaluation requires holdout precision (n≈30+), not literature validation of 2-3 examples. cancer cross-type overlap promotion was the single largest source of noise in MEDIUM tier.

learnings.learning: h487 mechanism split for psychiatric (0% nomech) was a small-n artifact (n=1.3/seed). Actual replication: 10% from n=2.4/seed. 46.2% full-data GT rate = most are FDA-approved uses. +0.2pp MEDIUM impact not worth clinical false positives.
learnings.implication: Always verify sub-rule splits have n>=5/seed before making demotion decisions. Full-data GT rate is a useful cross-check when holdout is unreliable.

learnings.learning: Audited all 8 implemented holdout-based decisions. 2 were technically unreliable (hematological n=4.9, reproductive only 1 seed) but both correct by full-data + clinical review. 34%+ of sub-rule holdouts have n<5/seed. Conservative multi-evidence approach = robust to artifacts.
learnings.implication: For future decisions: always require full-data + clinical support when holdout n<5. Sub-rule splitting creates fragmentation - only split at n>25 full-data. The system's integrity is confirmed.

learnings.learning: CCB audit found 4 harmful predictions (diltiazem cardiac arrest, verapamil CHF, diltiazem VT, nifedipine ACS). Also discovered confidence_filter.py is NOT used by production_predictor.py - separate systems with potential safety gaps. INVERSE_INDICATION_PAIRS is the correct production safety mechanism.
learnings.implication: Need to audit ALL confidence_filter.py safety rules for coverage in production_predictor.py (h495). Class-level drug safety audits (like CCBs) are efficient: one audit covers multiple harmful predictions.

learnings.learning: confidence_filter.py and production_predictor.py are independent systems with 80% safety rule gap. Class Ic antiarrhythmics (CAST trial) and SGLT2i→hypoglycemia were the main uncovered harmful patterns. Always cross-reference safety systems after changes.
learnings.implication: When adding inverse indication rules, check BOTH systems. Consider migrating all confidence_filter.py rules to INVERSE_INDICATION_PAIRS for single source of truth.

learnings.learning: GOLDEN 'standard' rule (34% of GOLDEN) has higher false positive risk than hierarchy rules. Lidocaine freq=43 leads to many false positives but also many correct predictions. Individual prediction exclusions = overfitting. Minocycline CAUSES urticaria (case reports).
learnings.implication: Consider a holdout audit specifically for 'standard' rule GOLDEN predictions vs hierarchy GOLDEN. May warrant a slight frequency threshold increase for standard rule.

learnings.learning: expanded_ground_truth.json was missing 1503 drug-disease pairs from the production predictor's GT (built from Every Cure Excel via fuzzy matching). This caused ALL holdout precision numbers to be pessimistic by ~7-8pp for HIGH/MEDIUM. After syncing, holdout: GOLDEN 67%, HIGH 61%, MEDIUM 31%, LOW 15%, FILTER 10%.
learnings.implication: Always keep expanded GT in sync with production GT. When GT source data changes, re-sync before running holdout evaluation. Full-data precision is now much higher than holdout (22pp gap for GOLDEN) - use holdout as authoritative.

learnings.learning: Standard GOLDEN (62.2% holdout) and Hierarchy GOLDEN (70.3% holdout) are NOT significantly different (p>0.35). Full-data gap (standard 55.7% vs hierarchy 89.5%) is mostly hierarchy overfitting. No demotion needed.
learnings.implication: GOLDEN tier is well-justified for both rule types. Hierarchy full-data precision is inflated.

learnings.learning: kNN predictions were non-deterministic across Python processes due to dict iteration order for tied scores. Fixed with drug_id tiebreaker.
learnings.implication: Always use a deterministic tiebreaker when sorting by float scores. Python dict ordering is process-dependent.

learnings.learning: CV standard MEDIUM has 2.0% holdout (essentially random). cv_pathway_comprehensive 44pp gap is from disease selection variance, NOT overfitting. PAH is 100% self-referential.
learnings.implication: Category-level MEDIUM demotions should check sub-rule granularity. Self-referential diseases need systematic identification.

learnings.learning: 31.6% of diseases are 100% self-referential in kNN. This is structural: their drugs are not shared with ANY neighbor. MEDIUM holdout drops from 40.8% (<50% self-ref) to 13.3% (100% self-ref). Not actionable as a demotion because self-ref requires GT knowledge.
learnings.implication: kNN has a structural floor for ~144 diseases. External data needed for these diseases. Self-referentiality is the dominant source of full-to-holdout gap.

learnings.learning: Seed 42 poor performance is sampling variance: fewest autoimmune (3), most infectious (22), lowest mean GT (5.2). 5-seed evaluation has ±20% GOLDEN variance. Stratified splitting would help but adds complexity.
learnings.implication: Report results as mean±std across seeds. Individual seed outliers are expected with n=91 holdout diseases.

learnings.learning: GT-free embedding features (same_cat_frac AUC=0.734, embedding_norm AUC=0.657) correlate well with self-referentiality on full data but REVERSE on holdout (gap -6.0pp ± 12.9pp). Root cause: low same_cat_frac captures TWO opposite populations (58% self-referential + 42% cross-category transfer). This is another instance of the collider/full-to-holdout reversal pattern (h453/h445).
learnings.implication: Self-referentiality is a structural floor of kNN that cannot be detected or corrected without GT knowledge. Alternative similarity measures (HPO, gene overlap) needed for 144 structurally un-generalizable diseases.

learnings.learning: GT completeness audit: only 15/167 FDA-approved pairs missing across 20 major diseases. 14/15 not in model's top-30 predictions. GT incompleteness is NOT the precision bottleneck. Holdout baseline has drifted: GOLDEN 63.3% (not 67.0%), HIGH 51.5% (not 60.8%), MEDIUM 29.9% (not 32.1%) due to accumulated code changes since h478.
learnings.implication: Future GT expansion has diminishing returns for major categories. Model structural improvements (external data, HPO similarity, multi-graph) needed for further precision gains. CLAUDE.md holdout numbers need periodic re-validation after code changes.

learnings.learning: CV hierarchy groups are all too small for holdout validation (3-5 diseases each). Full-data precision is high (65-93%) confirming genuine medical knowledge. h506's 35.1% coronary holdout was from n≈1 disease/seed.
learnings.implication: Stop investigating individual hierarchy group demotions when group size < 10 diseases. Small hierarchy rules should be evaluated on full-data precision only.

learnings.learning: Self-referentiality has two distinct causes: small GT (79%, OR=8.6x) and therapeutic islands (8%, dedicated drug classes). GI/immunological 89-100% self-ref vs autoimmune/dermatological 20-33%. Mechanism-specific overlap minimal (4.2%).
learnings.implication: GT size is the dominant predictor of self-referentiality. Therapeutic islands (PAH, HepC, CKD) are informative for annotation but not actionable for demotion.

learnings.learning: Automated literature status classification using 17 drug class SOC mappings achieves +28.4pp precision lift in HIGH tier. Covers 11.7% of predictions as LIKELY_GT_GAP. Top classes: corticosteroids, cancer drugs, fluoroquinolones. Implementation is conservative and clinically reasonable.
learnings.implication: SOC classification is a reliable annotation for deliverable consumers. Potential for tier promotion but needs holdout validation first.

learnings.learning: SOC signal is heterogeneous: corticosteroids drive nearly all of the +6pp MEDIUM lift. Non-hematological corticosteroid MEDIUM = 50.1% holdout, comparable to HIGH. Promotion implemented: +2.3pp HIGH, +1.2pp MEDIUM. Most other SOC classes have tiny-n (<10/seed) making them unactionable individually.
learnings.implication: Drug-class-specific SOC promotions can improve tier precision when medical rationale is clear and n is sufficient. Hematological category is consistently weaker for corticosteroids.

learnings.learning: Hematological corticosteroid demotion gives small but consistent improvements. Medical rationale solid: corticosteroids treat autoimmune blood disorders but not genetic ones. Pattern: when a drug class has clear category-specific efficacy differences, category-specific tier rules are justified.
learnings.implication: Consider similar category-specific rules for other drug-category pairs with heterogeneous outcomes.

learnings.learning: Self-referential percentage is a strong predictor of holdout precision (25.2% vs 6.0% gradient). But it requires GT knowledge so cannot be used for tier assignment. Best used as deliverable annotation for downstream consumers.
learnings.implication: Any future GT-free proxy for self-referentiality would be extremely valuable for tier improvement.

learnings.learning: SIDER adverse effect mining requires strict matching + indication cross-check + manual medical audit. Loose substring matching produces 80%+ false positives. Generic AE terms (ulcer, infection, tension) match disease names that the drug actually TREATS. The SIDER indications file is essential for excluding known treatments.
learnings.implication: Any future AE-based filtering must use exact/near-exact disease matching and cross-check against indication databases. Short AE terms (<8 chars) should be excluded entirely.

learnings.learning: SIDER indications are ~66% noise even for NLP_indication labels. Only exact name matching + manual medical audit produces reliable GT expansion. Most noise is from comorbidity mentions in clinical trial descriptions (e.g., drugs for diabetes patients also mention hypertension, ACS, etc.).
learnings.implication: Automated GT expansion from SIDER requires strict filtering. Best approach: NLP_indication only + exact matching + medical audit. ~1/3 candidates are genuine.

learnings.learning: Inverse indication filter ordering matters: safety-critical checks must precede all positive tier assignments. Cancer_same_type was bypassing inverse_indication check. 38 GT entries are actually inverse indications (drug CAUSES disease).
learnings.implication: Always place safety filters at the TOP of _assign_confidence_tier. GT quality issues can be masked by inverse indication filters.

learnings.learning: DRKG associations ≠ treatments. 19 DRKG-derived GT entries were actually inverse indications (drug causes disease). Always validate DRKG associations against clinical evidence before including in GT.
learnings.implication: Future GT expansion should cross-check against inverse indication list. Every Cure GT has ~5 incorrect entries (adverse effects labeled as indications) and ~8 disease name mismatch errors.

learnings.learning: FILTER tier is well-calibrated. rank>20 = 80% of FILTER, no category rescue works. TransE consilience provides +6.3pp holdout within FILTER but only 16.3% total (= LOW level, not worth promoting). Full-data TransE shows no signal; only holdout differentiates.
learnings.implication: FILTER tier boundary is robust. Future improvements must come from improving the underlying kNN model, not from reclassifying existing FILTER predictions.

learnings.learning: Cancer drug MEDIUM tier is well-calibrated. Cytotoxic drugs (anthracyclines 73%, taxanes 71%, antimetabolites 48%) have higher precision than targeted therapy (kinase inhibitors 10%), but at 53% overall they fall BETWEEN MEDIUM (28.8%) and HIGH (58.5%). Promoting would dilute HIGH. They are in the correct tier.
learnings.implication: Do NOT attempt cancer drug sub-stratification for tier promotion. The cancer_same_type MEDIUM rule is optimal. Focus on targeted therapy demotions if anything (kinase_inhibitors at 9.6% could be LOW).

learnings.learning: Literature audit of top 50 GOLDEN/HIGH novel predictions: 58% strongly validated, 88% reasonable. GOLDEN 100% reasonable, HIGH 80%. Three error patterns: local anesthetic procedural artifacts (27/29 HIGH), wrong antibiotic spectrum (5 predictions), statin→diabetes inverse indication (5 predictions). Added statin→diabetes to inverse indication filter.
learnings.implication: Deliverable quality is high. Largest improvement: filter local anesthetic procedural artifacts from GOLDEN/HIGH (h540). Antibiotic spectrum is minor issue.

learnings.learning: Local anesthetic (lidocaine/bupivacaine) predictions in non-pain disease categories are procedural artifacts from KG co-occurrence. Demoting to LOW improved all tiers (HIGH +0.3pp, MEDIUM +0.2pp). 132 predictions moved. GT itself has ~16 false LA indications from DRKG.
learnings.implication: KG procedural co-occurrence is a systematic bias. Consider auditing other drug classes with primarily procedural use (contrast agents, surgical drugs, etc.).

learnings.learning: HIGH tier is 74.6% corticosteroid novel predictions due to h520 SOC promotion. This is correct (50% holdout) but poor diversity. Users need drug class annotation to filter. Not an error to fix.
learnings.implication: Consider adding drug_class column to deliverable. Also consider limiting corticosteroid predictions to max 2-3 per disease to improve diversity without losing precision.

learnings.learning: Anti-TNF biologics (adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab) INDUCE autoimmune conditions including SLE (12K FAERS reports), MG (case reports), and MS (paradoxical demyelination). These are NOT treatments but inverse indications. Must add to INVERSE_INDICATION_PAIRS.
learnings.implication: All anti-TNF predictions for autoimmune diseases should be scrutinized for paradoxical autoimmune induction. Need comprehensive anti-TNF audit (h544).

learnings.learning: 86% of novel GOLDEN/HIGH skin/autoimmune predictions are corticosteroids — clinically valid but not novel. Only 14% are mechanistically specific (anti-TNF, anti-CD20, immunosuppressants). For collaboration value, focus on non-corticosteroid predictions.
learnings.implication: Deliverable utility is diluted by corticosteroid dominance. Consider class-level grouping (h547) to highlight genuinely novel predictions.

learnings.learning: Drug-target/disease-gene overlap is a strong within-tier holdout signal (+11.4pp MEDIUM novel) but NOT sufficient for tier promotion (27.1% << HIGH 58.9%). Partially circular with kNN (same DRKG edges). Strongest for gene-poor diseases (+16.7pp). Implemented as annotation column.
learnings.implication: Gene overlap is useful for human review and experimental prioritization, but adds limited ML value due to circularity with kNN. Future work: test with EXTERNAL gene databases (DisGeNET) that aren't in DRKG.

learnings.learning: Anti-TNF paradoxical autoimmunity is a CLASS EFFECT: all agents (adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab, golimumab) can induce SLE, MS, autoimmune hepatitis, sarcoidosis, vasculitis. Drug-specific effects exist too (adalimumab→polymyositis/lichen planus). Etanercept has highest sarcoidosis/vasculitis risk, infliximab has highest AIH risk. Anti-TNF can paradoxically both TREAT and INDUCE eczema, but eczema is manageable with topicals.
learnings.implication: Every anti-TNF prediction for autoimmune conditions should be scrutinized. Some diseases (GVHD, TEN) are correctly TREATED by anti-TNF despite being autoimmune/immune-mediated.

learnings.learning: MEDIUM tier is 56% reasonable vs 88% for GOLDEN/HIGH - confirming tier system calibration. Main MEDIUM error patterns: wrong cancer subtype (cancer_same_type overgeneralizes), wrong antibiotic spectrum, and diagnostic agent artifacts. FDG (PET tracer) had 55 false predictions.
learnings.implication: Cancer same-type and antibiotic spectrum are the two biggest remaining quality gaps in MEDIUM tier.

learnings.learning: MEDIUM tier has heterogeneous per-category precision: psychiatric 54.8%, musculoskeletal 53.8% vs hematological 10.0%, metabolic 18.0%. Hematological default MEDIUM is 0% on holdout. Metabolic statin/TZD rescue for non-hierarchy diseases is 8.3% — below LOW. Sub-reason analysis more informative than category-level: target_overlap_promotion (45.3%) is HIGH-quality within MEDIUM.
learnings.implication: Consider promoting target_overlap_promotion from MEDIUM to HIGH (h554). For categories, only hematological warranted full demotion; metabolic is heterogeneous and requires rule-level intervention.

learnings.learning: Antibiotic→viral disease predictions are systematically wrong (3.3% full-data, 5.0% holdout). Antibiotics cannot treat viral infections. The kNN co-prescription artifact inflates scores. 35 predictions caught by rule. Corticosteroid→infectious is more nuanced (12.1% holdout) — valid for inflammatory responses to infections (zoster, leprosy, ABPA) but not for direct infection treatment.
learnings.implication: Simple drug-class/pathogen-type mismatch rules can catch clear biological errors. More nuanced rules (corticosteroid exceptions) require disease-specific lists.

learnings.learning: Within default MEDIUM, rank is the strongest predictor: 1-5 (38.7%) → 6-10 (24.0%) → 11-20 (18.7-20.7%). Mechanism support adds +14pp. Frequency-only MEDIUM at high rank is LOW-quality. The freq>=10 no-mechanism path is the bulk of MEDIUM predictions (144/seed) and performs below average.
learnings.implication: Rank within kNN top-20 is a continuous signal, not just a binary cutoff. High-rank + mechanism = HIGH-quality MEDIUM; low-rank + no-mechanism = LOW-quality.

learnings.learning: CS→infectious MEDIUM has 2.1% holdout — even medically valid uses (ABPA, zoster, leprosy, TB) don't generalize. Medical validity doesn't predict GT hit rate for rare drug-disease combinations. KG co-occurrence from procedural use dominates.
learnings.implication: Don't assume medical plausibility implies holdout performance. Always measure even when clinical literature supports the combination.

learnings.learning: MEDIUM precision ceiling at 34.2% via demotion strategy. cancer_same_type (27.9%, 39% of MEDIUM) is the main drag but at genuine MEDIUM level. No remaining sub-reasons with both low holdout (<25%) and high n (>=10/seed). Further improvement requires promotion or refinement, not demotion.
learnings.implication: Pivot from demotion to refinement strategies. cancer_same_type subtype specificity is the highest-impact remaining direction.

learnings.learning: Short abbreviation keywords (ALL, CLL, AML, CML) in substring matching cause false positives. 'all' matches 'small', 'fallopian', 'allergic'. Always use word boundary matching for keywords <=4 chars. This bug affected 8 diseases and 39 cancer_same_type predictions.
learnings.implication: Audit all substring matching in the codebase for short keyword false positives. Use regex word boundaries for abbreviations.

learnings.learning: Antimicrobial-pathogen mismatch is a clean 0% holdout signal. Drug class × pathogen type is a strong biological rule. Dual-activity drugs (metronidazole, doxycycline, amphotericin B) must be handled carefully. Target_overlap promotion can rescue predictions that should stay demoted — always check for leakage paths.
learnings.implication: Look for similar drug-class × disease-subtype mismatches in other categories. Always check if target_overlap or other promotion paths override demotions.

learnings.learning: 37% of diseases have 0% holdout. 80% of these have GT≤2 (structural small-GT limit). The remaining 20% are therapeutic islands where drug profiles are too specific for kNN. Top performers are large-GT autoimmune diseases with many shared drugs (RA=93%, UC=67%).
learnings.implication: Disease-level confidence annotation would help clinicians. Therapeutic islands need alternative prediction strategies.

learnings.learning: Node2Vec DRKG embeddings cluster diseases by shared drug patterns, NOT by disease category. 91% of diseases have <20% same-category among k=20 neighbors. Category coherence has zero correlation with holdout precision (r=-0.002). Quality signals must exploit the drug-sharing structure, not categorical structure.
learnings.implication: Any embedding-based quality signal should be based on drug overlap, not category overlap. The kNN works because similar diseases share drugs, not because they're in the same category.

learnings.learning: Comprehensive drug-class × disease-category mismatch scan found NO new actionable rules beyond existing filters (ATC mismatch, domain-isolated, antimicrobial, CS→infectious, statin/TZD). MEDIUM demotion ceiling confirmed at ~35.8%. Further MEDIUM improvement requires promotions or entirely new signals.
learnings.implication: Demotion-based MEDIUM improvement is exhausted. Future work should focus on: (1) annotation quality signals, (2) novel prediction strategies, or (3) external data integration.

learnings.learning: kNN norm_score adds signal beyond rank for prediction quality. Within MEDIUM: Q4 (high score) = 28.2% vs Q1 (low score) = 12.6%. Not GT-size proxy (r≈0). Captures neighborhood consensus. Already in deliverable as annotation.
learnings.implication: Users can use norm_score to prioritize within-tier. High norm_score predictions are more reliable. Score gap is redundant with norm_score (r=-0.716 with rank).

learnings.learning: Drug-sharing density (GT-derived) has partial r=0.448 with precision after controlling for GT size. But 93% of diseases have near-zero sharing with kNN neighbors. kNN generalizes when neighbors share drugs; fails when they don't. This is the structural limit of kNN — it can only transfer knowledge that exists in the training neighborhood.
learnings.implication: kNN works well for diseases embedded near drug-rich diseases with overlapping treatments. For diseases with unique treatment patterns (PAH, HCV, migraine), kNN structurally cannot help. Alternative prediction strategies needed for low-sharing diseases.

learnings.learning: HIGH-frequency corticosteroids (freq>=30) create persistent holdout artifacts. Their broad GT coverage means they hit GT for held-out diseases, inflating precision in any subgroup they appear. This makes LOW/FILTER sub-population analysis unreliable when CS predictions are included. Always separate CS vs non-CS when analyzing sub-populations.
learnings.implication: Must always control for corticosteroid presence when measuring sub-population holdout precision. Report CS-free metrics alongside total metrics.

learnings.finding: HIGH-frequency corticosteroids (freq>=30) create persistent holdout artifacts. Their broad GT coverage inflates precision in any subgroup they appear. Always separate CS vs non-CS when analyzing sub-populations.
